prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, which brought optical frequency standards to a fractional uncertainty near 1e-18

statement.case_for: My opening view holds after reading the other seven ballots. The optical lattice clock is an idea (magic-wavelength trapping, which cancels the light shift of the clock transition while many atoms are interrogated at once) carried through to a measured result: independent laboratories now compare clocks at the 1e-18 level, far beyond the caesium standard, and the community is preparing a redefinition of the second. It also yields physics beyond metrology, such as gravitational redshift resolved over millimetres, bounds on drifting constants and sensitivity to certain dark-sector couplings. The credited pair maps onto the achievement without strain: Katori for the magic-wavelength proposal and first Sr lattice clock, Ye for the accuracy and stability demonstrations and the many-body clock regime. All eight members place the candidate in their top six and six place it in their top three, so support is broad rather than concentrated. Few other shortlisted candidates combine a clean one-or-two-person credit with full maturity.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the field has already been honoured twice nearby: Hall and Hänsch (2005, frequency comb) and Wineland and Haroche (2012, quantum control of single ions, which also underlies ion clocks). A sceptical reader may call lattice clocks an engineering refinement of tools already rewarded, and metrology rather than a discovery. Contributions from other lattice-clock and ion-clock groups (SYRTE, PTB, NIST ion clocks) are also not captured by the two supplied names, and the relative weight of Katori's proposal against Ye's accuracy programme cannot be settled from the supplied text.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B053 first and argues that the pair is cleanly separable from the comb and ion-clock prizes, with strong multi-laboratory confirmation and a redefinition of the second under discussion.
responses.response: I agree on confirmation and on the credit mapping, but I would not call the separation from the 2005 and 2012 prizes clean. A magic-wavelength lattice makes a neutral-atom ensemble clock work in a way a single trapped ion cannot (statistics scale with atom number, and Ye's Fermi-degenerate clocks add many-body shifts to control), and that is the distinction the citation should state explicitly. Without it the overlap objection is stronger than Kroll's note allows, and I would write the citation around the lattice scheme, not around accuracy alone.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube first for opening a new observational window, and ranks B053 second while asking whether clocks are metrology rather than discovery, a question of taste.
responses.response: I take the neutrino case seriously: the diffuse flux is secure and a new window is a classic Nobel pattern. But the three-person credit is the weak point in a collaboration of several hundred, and Pearce himself notes that source identifications remain at modest significance and that the credit weighting is unsettled. On the metrology point I disagree that it is only taste: the statutes' emphasis on discovery or invention fits here, because the invention is paired with measured consequences, including gravitational redshift tests and constants bounds. If the committee prefers an observational discovery I would accept B009 as an alternative, but I would not rank it above B053 while credit among Halzen, Karle and Spiering is unresolved.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the experimental Higgs discovery first as the natural complement to the 2013 theory prize, while admitting that choosing three among four leaders of two collaborations is a real compromise.
responses.response: I accept the scientific importance without reservation. My difficulty is the same one Danielsson states: the discovery belongs to two collaborations of thousands, so any three names are a partly arbitrary representation, and the committee would be choosing among Gianotti, Jenni, Virdee and Della Negra on role rather than on scientific contribution. The clock case fits the three-person limit far better. I would keep B046 as a serious candidate but cannot support it as preferred while the allocation is this contested.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first, holding that it complements the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in circuits without duplicating it, and that its influence on quantum processors is very high.
responses.response: I agree that circuit QED is foundational and that Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf are a coherent theory-plus-experiment trio. Where I differ is timing: the 2025 prize went to circuit quantum behaviour in the same community, so awarding superconducting circuits again one year later would, in my judgement, weigh against it, and Girvin and Devoret are missing from the credit (Johansson notes this too). I rank it below the clocks for that reason, and it remains outside my alternatives only because B013 and B033 carry cleaner attribution.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first, calling the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by experimental confirmation a clean theory-experiment arc, and treats the unresolved pairing mechanism as not undermining the core discovery.
responses.response: I share the view that the prediction-plus-discovery structure is clean and that Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero is a natural trio; that is why B033 is among my alternatives. I would still give more weight than Eriksson to maturity: the superconducting pairing mechanism and device-to-device variability are open, and Cao and the other experimental co-workers are absent from the credit. Condensed matter is also outside my field, so I defer to colleagues who know the experiments better, but on the evidence supplied I would let the field settle before honouring it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards optical lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize on controlled single ions.
How to weight Katori's magic-wavelength proposal against Ye's accuracy and many-body programme; the supplied credit pairs them but cannot settle relative contribution.
I have not independently verified the latest published clock uncertainty and comparison figures.
Contributions of uncredited groups (SYRTE, PTB, NIST) to lattice-clock development cannot be added within the supplied credit.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B053: my profile documents no collaboration with Katori or Ye. I work in atomic theory and have an extended collaboration with Anne L'Huillier and the Lund attosecond group, plus collaborations with Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich; none of this involves the credited names of the shortlisted candidates, but my field proximity to atomic and optical physics should be disclosed as a possible source of bias towards B053.
